div.head: Editorial Principles
div.p: This page records the editorial decisions taken in the making of eLiebermann, and the methods by which its texts have been transcribed, checked and encoded. It is revised as the work proceeds. For an account of the project, of Felix Liebermann and his Gesetze, and of how to cite eLiebermann, see About.

div.head: General
Aims and scope
div.p: eLiebermann has been built from spreadsheets and transcriptions compiled over a number of years for the editor's research on the language and composition of the early English laws, and its structure, corrections and indexing reflect the questions that this research has asked of the texts. It is offered here in the hope that it may be of wider use to others working on the laws and their language.

The Lawcodes Database is concerned principally with the Old English laws issued before 1066, and its record of these codes is the most complete. It also reproduces the majority of the other legal and quasi-legal texts that Liebermann prints, including some post-Conquest codes and compilations. The Legal Dictionary is an edition of the whole of Liebermann's Wörterbuch.
div.head: Liebermann and beyond
div.p: The project takes its name from Felix Liebermann, and his Gesetze der Angelsachsen is its foundation: his texts, his German translation, his apparatus and his clause divisions are the frame to which everything else is fitted.

The project aims, however, to be more than a digital reproduction of the Gesetze. It gathers beside Liebermann's text the editions and translations of later scholars, where these can be reproduced; it directs readers by page number to more recent editions of Liebermann's clauses; it organises and corrects the texts, checking them against the printed volumes and against Liebermann's own textual notes and corrections; it records cross-references between clauses drawn from Liebermann's margins and from the scholarship of the following century; and it adds a subject index of the laws that is the editor's own. Where the site corrects or adds to Liebermann, this is noted.
div.head: The base text
div.p: Liebermann's text is reproduced as he printed it, with his sigla, his numbering and his typography. Every dictionary entry and every lawcode clause page is linked to its page in a scan of the printed volume (on archive.org), so that any reading may be verified against the original.
div.head: Method and Data
div.p: The editorial work combines the editor's transcriptions, corrections and scholarship with machine-assisted transcription, collation and encoding.

Every dictionary entry and every lawcode clause is a separate file in TEI XML, the international standard for scholarly digital editions (Text Encoding Initiative, P5). All the project's text and data are kept under version control in a Git repository, in which every addition or correction, whether made by hand or by script, is proposed as a separate, documented change and published after review.

div.head: The Legal Dictionary
Transcription and collation
div.p: Every dictionary entry has been transcribed twice, independently. The project team keyed all entries by hand; a second transcription was made in 2026 from page images of the Wörterbuch by Claude, a large language model developed by Anthropic. The two transcriptions have been collated entry by entry and word by word. Each disagreement is classified (a slip in one transcription or the other, a difference of typography only, or a different division between entries) and, where it cannot be settled from the transcriptions alone, is checked by the editor against the printed volume. A report of each collation, and a running list of readings still to be checked against the print, are kept with the project's data.
div.head: Typography
div.p: Liebermann's typography carries meaning: roman type is the language of the laws; italic is Liebermann's German and his grammatical commentary; bold marks headwords; and a superscript L or F marks a Latin or French word. This system is preserved in the transcriptions, and has occasionally been regularised where Liebermann's own practice is inconsistent. Page breaks are recorded, so that each entry is linked to its page in the printed volume.
div.head: Abbreviations, technical terms and conventional signs
div.p: Liebermann's Wörterbuch relies on a dense system of abbreviations, grammatical terms and conventional signs, which Liebermann nowhere sets out in full. The list of Grammatical Terms and Abbreviations, and the pop-ups drawn from it throughout the dictionary, are the editor's reconstruction of that system. Each item gives (i) the German form as Liebermann wrote it out, or as he would have written it out; (ii) the modern standard German equivalent, where the spelling or the word itself has since changed; and (iii) an English translation; with notes where needed.

Where Liebermann gives no expansion, the meaning has been inferred from his usage. Every one of the c. 500 abbreviations (639 forms in all) has been checked against its occurrences across the entries. An exclamation mark after a quoted form, for example, which Liebermann does not explain, is taken to mean sic, since it appears where a manuscript has an unexpected or incorrect form (an accusative ending, say, where a dative would be expected).

Liebermann is not wholly consistent in either his terminology or his abbreviations. One term may appear in more than one abbreviated form, and one abbreviation may serve for more than one term: sbj stands for "subject" in the grammatical notes but for "subjunctive" in the Old French entries. Some expansions offered here are therefore necessarily provisional. The list is meant as an aid to Liebermann's technical and explanatory vocabulary, not as a glossary of the ordinary German of his definitions, whose words are accordingly not linked. Corrections are welcome through the Suggest a change box at the foot of each dictionary entry.

Law-code sigla, manuscript sigla and grammatical abbreviations within an entry are identified automatically in the first instance, by longest match against the authority lists compiled by the editor, and linked to their expansions. In those frequent cases where Liebermann further shortens his abbreviations or citations and automatic linking is not possible, the editor has created the relevant links. Finding and correcting missing or incorrect links is an ongoing process; corrections are welcome through the Suggest a change box at the foot of each dictionary entry, which has an option for missing or wrong links.
div.head: Citations of the laws
div.p: Each citation of a law in an entry is normalised to a standard key (law code and clause number, following the usual scholarly form of citation) and linked to that clause in the Lawcodes Database.
div.head: Authors and works cited
div.p: Liebermann prints no bibliography, and cites modern scholarship and editions by short title. The full citations on the list of Authors and Works Cited have been reconstructed by the editor from those short titles, from the two brief lists of works in the Gesetze (I, p. LIV; II.2, p. 262), and from the editions current when he wrote. Where Liebermann cites a primary source without naming an edition, the edition he most probably used is given. These identifications are marked as provisional until they can be checked against the editions themselves.
div.head: Cross-reference and spelling entries
div.p: Liebermann's own cross-references between entries (s. WORD) are given as links. An entry that serves only to send the reader to another headword is shown with the headword or headwords to which it refers, without the further apparatus of a full entry. Headwords that record orthographic variation rather than a distinct word (for example aa for ā) are marked as spelling entries.
div.head: Editorial corrections
div.p: Where Liebermann's printed entry is corrected (where, for example, it refers the reader to a headword that does not exist, or to an incorrect spelling), the change is explained in an Editor's note on the entry page.
div.head: Other dictionaries
div.p: Where possible, Old English headwords are linked to the corresponding entries in the Bosworth–Toller Anglo-Saxon Dictionary and in the Dictionary of Old English (DOE). The links to both dictionaries were first made by a semi-automated process: Liebermann's headwords were matched against the dictionaries' own headwords, allowing for the usual variations of Old English spelling and for Liebermann's practice of heading an entry with the form found in the laws rather than the dictionary form, and the matches were then graded by their likelihood. Matches of which there is any doubt, and headwords for which no match is found, are reviewed by the editor, and the remaining links are being checked; until they have been, some may be erroneous. Corrections and missing links may be reported through the Suggest a change box at the foot of each dictionary entry.

The DOE has so far been published for the letters A to Le, and only entries within that range can be linked to it. It is available by subscription, at different addresses for institutional and individual subscribers; readers may choose which on any entry page, and the choice is remembered by their browser.

div.head: The Lawcodes Database
Compilation
div.p: The database is compiled in a master spreadsheet of more than fifty fields for each clause, from which the clause files are generated by script. For every clause the spreadsheet records at least Liebermann's text of each manuscript he prints, identified by his siglum, with his page number; his German translation; and an English rendering of his German.
div.head: Clause division
div.p: Liebermann's division of the laws into clauses is followed throughout, so that every citation of the form used by Liebermann and by the scholarship that depends on him leads to a single clause. The texts of later editions are divided at Liebermann's clause breaks, including those printed by their editors as continuous prose. Where a later editor divides a clause more finely, the clause is kept whole and the editor's divisions are marked within it by that editor's own numbers.
div.head: Clause numbers
div.p: This edition divides and numbers the laws as Liebermann does in Die Gesetze der Angelsachsen. These are the citations he uses throughout his Wörterbuch, and in all the notes throughout his edition. They are also the citations used in a century of scholarship, and keeping them means that every citation in the dictionary, and in most of the secondary literature, leads to the right clause.

The numbers, and the editorial divisions upon which they are based, have well-known faults. For the earlier codes Liebermann adopted the divisions of Schmid and Thorpe, which follow the manuscript rubrics, and are often at odds with the sense. He kept them even where he disagreed, and in places recorded where he would have divided otherwise. Later scholars have expressed increasing frustration with the flaws of this system. Wormald called the continued use of the received numbering of Æthelstan’s laws, “that everyone at least since 1858 has known to be wrong”, a sign of “the enslavement of early English legal studies to traditional practice” (The Making of English Law, p. 291 n. 129). Richard Dammery’s doctoral edition of Alfred and Ine (1990) kept the old numbers but offered alternatives. Lisi Oliver’s edition of the Kentish laws (2002) and Jurasinski and Oliver’s of Alfred and Ine (2021) – now the standard texts of their respective codes – renumber outright.

The divisions are not a merely technical matter; they affect how the codes are to be read and understood. The decision to keep to Liebermann’s system here is nonetheless a technical one, and implies no judgement in its favour. eLiebermann is built around Liebermann’s Wörterbuch, whose many thousands of citations give his numbers; the links from each dictionary entry to the clauses it cites, Liebermann’s own cross-references and notes, and the cross-references collected from later scholarship all depend on a single, stable set of numbers, and that set can only be his.

Where a modern editor divides one of Liebermann’s clauses, the clause is kept whole here and the editor’s divisions are marked within it, with the editor’s own numbers. Wherever an editor numbers a clause differently, that number is shown in a grey bubble at the start of the editor’s text. Readers citing a modern edition should use its numbers. Readers citing this site, or Liebermann, should use his.
div.head: Manuscripts
div.p: Every text is identified by the manuscript from which it is taken, under Liebermann's siglum. Where Liebermann prints the text from more than one manuscript, his main text (taken to be that in his leftmost column) is given first.
div.head: Liebermann’s kinds of type
div.p: Liebermann uses the look of the print itself to tell the reader how a text relates to its source (Gesetze I, Vorrede pp. V–VI). These signs are being recorded and shown on the clause pages, beginning with the Instituta Cnuti. To keep the text readable they are shown quietly rather than in Liebermann’s own typography: plain black type is a faithful translation, and against it a pale wash marks what is changed in content, a fine grey underline what is reworded, grey type what is taken word for word from the source, and a dotted underline in brackets the other version. Hovering over a marked word gives a one- or two-word reminder (Changed, Reworded, From source, Other version), and a key stands above each text that has them.

list.item: Bold type, in a translation printed beside its source: the translation departs from the source in content (it adds, or says something different).
Spaced type: the translation departs from the source on purpose in form (it rewords).

Smaller type: words taken over word for word from an earlier law, named in Liebermann’s margin. In laws that survive in Old English he marks this in his German translation; in texts that survive only in Latin, in the Latin itself.

Round brackets ( ) in the Instituta Cnuti and Quadripartitus: two versions of the same words, an earlier and a later, which Liebermann thought were both the author’s own, so that he printed both in the text.

div.p: Liebermann did not mark omissions, and he used bold only for the larger changes (Bruce O’Brien, ‘The Instituta Cnuti and the Translation of English Law’, Anglo-Norman Studies 25 (2003), 177–97, at p. 181). An unmarked passage is therefore not necessarily a faithful translation.
div.head: Later editions
div.p: The texts and translations of later editions are entered with their page references, and are in the process of being re-checked against the printed books.
div.head: Translations
div.p: On each clause page Liebermann's German translation is given first, followed by the translations of modern editors, each attributed. The English cribs made for this site, of Liebermann's German and of the texts he left untranslated, are described under New Translations below.
div.head: Liebermann's notes
div.p: Liebermann's textual notes and his commentary (the Erklärungen of volume III) are given in the form of notes linked to his German translation, as printed. Each is accompanied by an English crib (see New Translations). These notes are hidden by default, to be shown clause by clause. Note that much of this commentary, and many of the legal comparisons Liebermann draws, have been superseded by later scholarship.
div.head: Cross-references between clauses
div.p: The early English legal corpus contains many laws that repeat or draw upon earlier laws, and certain "early" laws are in fact later compositions attributed to earlier kings. A record of the similarities between clauses offers a means of tracing these features of legislative composition. Liebermann's marginal cross-references have accordingly been transcribed from the page images of volume I, and the cross-references and comparisons of later scholars collected from their studies, editions, footnotes and tables of sources. Each is given with its source and page, and is linked in both directions. The wording on each clause page distinguishes the references made at that clause from those made at other clauses that point to it. The record is not yet complete, and suggestions for additional links are welcome.
div.head: Subject index
div.p: Every clause has been read and indexed by the offences, people, places and other matters with which it deals. The index was made for this project and is independent of Liebermann's Rechts- und Sachglossar (volume II, part 2).
div.head: Record of checking
div.p: Checking is recorded clause by clause: the foot of each clause page states what has been checked, and against which page of which book. This work is ongoing, and the record on each clause will note when a final check has been made by a member of the project team. Errors may be reported through the Report a problem box at the foot of each clause page.

div.head: New Translations
English of Liebermann's German
div.p: Liebermann's German translation of the laws is accompanied on each clause page by a close, semi-literal English rendering, labelled English of Liebermann's German. It was made with the assistance of a large language model (Claude, developed by Anthropic, 2026). It renders Liebermann's German, with his choices of word and construction; it is not a translation of the Old English, Latin or French text from which his German was made.
div.head: English cribs of the untranslated texts
div.p: Liebermann gives no German translation of many of the Latin texts he prints, among them the Quadripartitus, the Instituta Cnuti, the Leges Henrici Primi, the Leges Edwardi Confessoris, the Consiliatio Cnuti, and the ordeal and excommunication formulae, nor of a few Old English and French texts. So that every clause in the database can be read in English, each of these texts has been given an English crib, labelled on the clause page English crib of the Latin (or of the Old English, of the French). Where a clause has texts from more than one manuscript, the crib names the manuscript whose text it renders. The crib of the Instituta Cnuti is also given in the continuous reading text of that work (Instituta Cnuti, read in order).

These cribs were made with the same large language model, working to a written brief. The brief asks for a semi-literal rendering that keeps close to the structure of the original, and for the formulae of Anglo-Latin law and of canon law to be rendered by their established English equivalents rather than paraphrased. Passages that recur within a text, or from one text to another, were translated together, so that they read alike. Words supplied for the sense stand in square brackets, as do Liebermann's own supplements. Where the text is doubtful, or the sense could not be construed with confidence, the crib marks the place with [?], and these places are listed for the editor to check.
div.head: English of Liebermann's notes
div.p: Liebermann's textual footnotes (Gesetze I) and his Erklärungen (Gesetze III) are each given in his German with an English crib made in the same way.
div.head: The status of the English cribs
div.p: The English cribs are aids to reading, offered to help users find their way through Liebermann's German and through texts that have no published translation. They are not part of the edition. The edited text of eLiebermann is the text of the laws in its original languages, together with Liebermann's German and his apparatus as he printed them: these alone have been transcribed, collated and checked in accordance with the principles set out on this page. The cribs have not been systematically revised. The editor has corrected some errors where these have been noticed, but the cribs may still misconstrue the syntax of the original, mistake its technical terms, or miss its sense, and they are uneven in quality.

The cribs should therefore not be cited or quoted as translations, nor relied upon in any argument that turns on the wording or meaning of a text. Readers should return in every case to the original text, and to the published translations of modern editors where these exist; these are given, with their attributions, on the clause pages.

div.head: What is Not Included
div.p: eLiebermann gives Liebermann's texts of the laws with his apparatus, his German translation and his notes, and the whole of his Wörterbuch. It does not reproduce the whole of the Gesetze, however, and readers should bear in mind what has been left out. The two principal omissions are the Rechts- und Sachglossar (volume II, part 2) and Liebermann's introductions to the individual codes (volume III). Both remain of value to scholars, and both should be consulted in the printed volumes. They have been omitted because they are the parts of the Gesetze in which scholarship has most moved on since Liebermann wrote, and to present them beside the texts without a commentary of comparable scope would risk giving them an authority they no longer have.
div.head: The Rechts- und Sachglossar
div.p: The Rechts- und Sachglossar, published in 1912 as the second part of volume II, is a dictionary of the law itself. Under German headwords arranged alphabetically, Liebermann gathers the evidence of the laws on each legal institution, office, offence, procedure and social group, cites the clauses on which it rests, and sets the English evidence beside that of other legal systems, especially those of the continental Germanic peoples. Some articles are brief; others are extended essays. The work is a synthesis of a kind no one has since attempted for the early English laws, and it remains a valuable guide to where the evidence on a subject is to be found.

Its interpretations, however, were shaped by the German school of legal history in which Liebermann worked. The Sachglossar tends to treat the laws as the record of a single, coherent body of Germanic law, to draw them together into a system that the texts themselves do not present, and to supply what the English evidence lacks from continental analogues. Much of this framework has since been questioned, and a great deal of the work on which a modern account of these subjects would rest has been done since 1912. The subject index of this site, made for the project, is independent of the Sachglossar.
div.head: The introductions to the codes
div.p: In volume III (1916), before his Erklärungen to each text, Liebermann gives an introduction to it, discussing its date, authorship, sources, manuscripts and language. These introductions are not reproduced. On almost every one of these questions they have been overtaken by later work: by the study of the manuscripts and of their transmission, by the recognition of Archbishop Wulfstan's part in the composition of the later Anglo-Saxon codes, and by the modern editions of individual codes. The law-code and clause pages of this site instead record the dates proposed by later scholars, the attributions to Wulfstan, and the modern editions and studies of each code.
